newsitem.title: FRANCE: Star-studded gala, Wenders film mark Cannes 50th.
newsitem.headline: Star-studded gala, Wenders film mark Cannes 50th.

text.p: The Cannes Film Festival celebrated its 50th birthday on Sunday with a special award to Swedish master Ingmar Bergman at a star-studded gala.

Stars mounting the red-carpeted steps of the Palais des Festivals, to the march of a Republican Guard fanfare, included Sylvester Stallone, Andie MacDowell, Martin Scorsese, Gina Lollobrigida, John Hurt and Jeremy Irons.
The gala opened with a music and dance show by Philippe Decoufle, who designed the Albertville Olympic games opening ceremony in 1992.
The reclusive Bergman refused to attend the ceremony, and his special Palm of Palms award was handed to his actresses Bibi Andersson and Liv Ullman.
Following the presentation, Wim Wenders unveiled his thriller "The End of Violence", the latest in this year's competition diet of brooding films.

French President Jacques Chirac, assuming a high profile during a tightly contested parliamentary election campaign, showed up in Cannes for lunch with the festival jury and a chance to appear before the cameras with big film stars.
The Gaullist head of state left before the evening jamboree, dedicated to the memory of Italian director Marco Ferreri who died in Paris on Friday of a heart attack.

Wenders, a Cannes veteran voted best director in 1987 for "Wings of Desire" and a member of the jury two years later, showed a tale of state-sanctioned violence and intrusive police surveillance of Los Angeles public life.
Violence, the bespectacled Wenders, 52, said before the screening, "is conceived, produced and distributed in this city. Los Angeles has a very particular rapport with violence."

Gabriel Byrne and MacDowell, whom Wenders discovered in Cannes in "Sex, Lies and Videotape", star in the movie featuring a former NASA computer programmer who tries to stop the FBI using a surveillance system he developed in an attempt to end violence in the city.
Bill Pullman plays a successful Hollywood producer of violent movies who is forced to go into hiding after the programmer crosses his path.

"All the characters are deeply affected by violence -- and violence happens -- but only before or after: we never indulge in exploiting violence or showing it," Wenders said of his first English-language production since Golden Palm winner "Paris, Texas".

"Though we wanted the film to be about violence, we didn't want violence to be part of the film's language...To describe a disease, you have to risk catching it," said Wenders, who wrote the script in just six weeks and shot the $6.5 million film in 28 days.
